summary: The Water demand calculator turns the population size, the water requirement per capita and more to ADD ratio into average water demand. It suits a footprint, a resource or an environmental change you want to size up. The panel waits for the button. Edit a field, press Calculate, and compare — one input at a time is enough to see what drives the answer.

sections.title: How does the Water demand calculator work?
sections.html:
The Water demand calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports average water demand in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the population size, the water requirement per capita, the maximum water demand and the PHD to ADD ratio.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Water demand calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Average water demand=(11 ÷ 10) × population size × water requirement per capita
Average water demand=maximum water demand ÷ MDD to ADD ratio
Average water demand=peak water demand ÷ PHD to ADD ratio

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Population size = 10, Water requirement per capita = 10 L/day, MDD to ADD ratio = 1.4 and PHD to ADD ratio = 2.3. Working through the relationship above gives Average water demand = 110 L/day, Maximum water demand = 154 L/day and Peak water demand = 253 L/s.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Average water demand = 110 L/day, Maximum water demand = 154 L/day and Peak water demand = 253 L/s should be roughly the size you expected from Population size = 10 and Water requirement per capita = 10 L/day.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Water demand calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Comparing two options on the same basis
  • Putting a headline figure into context
  • Sizing an environmental impact in familiar units
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the population size, the water requirement per capita and the maximum water demand — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html: • Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.

faq.q: What does the Water demand calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns average water demand, derived from the population size, the water requirement per capita and the maximum water demand. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Water demand calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the population size, the water requirement per capita, the maximum water demand and the PHD to ADD ratio, which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter water requirement per capita in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Water requirement per capita opens in liters per day and the chip beside it offers 39 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Average water demand = 110 L/day. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Water demand calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
